Q: __await__: may it be called several times and then wait again? A:

Just for the record, I typed some snippets into the REPL - the behavior of returning the same iterator, one that is exhausted after the first await, differ than that from a co-routine; Subsequent awaits on "spent" iterators will result in 'None' for the await expression:

In [4]: class A:
   ...:     def __init__(self):
   ...:         def inner():
   ...:             yield
   ...:             return 2
   ...:         self.inner = inner()
   ...:     def __await__(self):
   ...:         return self.inner
   ...: 

In [5]: a = A()

In [6]: await a
Out[6]: 2

In [7]: await a # None

In [8]: await a

In [9]: await a

In [10]: async def b(): # coroutine for comparison
    ...:     return 3
    ...: 

In [11]: c = b()

In [12]: await c
Out[12]: 3

In [13]: await c
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
RuntimeError                              Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[13], line 1
----> 1 await c

RuntimeError: cannot reuse already awaited coroutine

Q: Why does C++26 add `CHAR_WIDTH` when we already have `CHAR_BIT`? A:

CHAR_BIT means number of bits in a byte, while CHAR_WIDTH means width of the char type.

For char, both are always the same because a byte is defined as the size of char:

CHAR_BIT == CHAR_WIDTH

CHAR_WIDTH was added in C++26 mainly for consistency with other macros like INT_WIDTH, LONG_WIDTH, etc., making generic programming cleaner.

Q: Scala equivalent of Java's Number A:

The answer from @gzm0 is a static solution, where the type is checked at compile time. Here is a dynamic solution which casts the type at runtime:

def toDoubleDynamic(x: Any) = x match {
     case s: String => s.toDouble
     case jn: java.lang.Number => jn.doubleValue()
     case _ => throw new ClassCastException("cannot cast to double")
}

Its use case is to choose a correct type at runtime.

Q: AES-256-CBC Bad Decrypt A:

You need to supply an IV for CBC mode and it needs to be block size (16-bytes for AES). 'dogsarefun' is only 10-bytes so the remaining bytes are unspecified and may (probably are) garbage.

Since PKCS padding is the default and CBC mode is used an incorrect IV will result in incorrect padding on decryption probably with the error: routines:EVP_DecryptFinal_ex:bad decrypt.

Q: How to actually compress a .txt file after obtaining a Huffman encoding A:

Your resulting string of ASCII '0' and '1' characters is eight times bigger than it needs to be. You need to encode it into 1/8th as many bytes by putting every eight of those 0's and 1's into one byte at a time, and write that to the output compressed file.

To do this, you would read the string and append a bit at a time to an integer bit buffer. In C++, an unsigned variable. Use the << and '|' operators to shift the integer to the left and or a bit into the bottom for each character in your string. E.g. buf = (buf << 1) | (str[i] & 1). The & 1 extracts the low bit of the '0' and '1' characters, which is unsurprisingly 0 and 1.

Once you have eight bits in buf, then write that out and start over.

At the end you will often have less than eight bits left in buf. If there are n = 1..7 bits left in buf, then shift those up so the first one is at the top, buf <<= 8 - n, and then write out buf as the last byte.

That leaves some trailing zero bits in the output. If you do nothing about this, then you have the risk of the decoder interpreting those as another Huffman code. The best way to handle this is to add a symbol to your encoding that is the end-of-stream symbol. It will have a frequency of 1, since it will occur once at the end. Encode that symbol after the data. When the decoder sees that symbol, it knows to stop and ingnore the subsequent bits. Other ways are to prepend the stream with a count of symbols to follow, or end the stream with a 1 bit followed by zero bits to the bottom of the last byte. In the latter case, the decoder looks at the last byte of the input, finds the least significant 1 bit in that byte, and discards that 1 bit and the 0 bits below it.

For the decoder to work, it will also need a description of the Huffman code that was used. An easy and compact way to do that is to first send a description of the binary tree (using the approach above for sending bits), where the tree is recursively traversed, and for each branch writing a 0 bit if it goes to another branch, or a 1 bit followed by the eight bits of the symbol if it's a leaf. This representation is self-terminating. You can immediately follow those bits with the encoded bits.

Q: Python error "ImportError: No module named" A:

On a Unix-like system, also make sure that PYTHONPATH is configured correctly, especially that it has this format:

.:/usr/local/lib/python

(Mind the .: at the beginning, so that it can search on the current directory, too.)

It may also be in other locations, depending on the version:

.:/usr/lib/python
.:/usr/lib/python2.6
.:/usr/lib/python2.7 and etc.
